grammar.v2.topic04Goal: Connect actions and entities to objects, places, people and times.
grammar.v2.review04Body: Interpret each situation before choosing a particle, an existence form or a time expression.
grammar.v2.particle-wo-object.title: を — what the verb acts on
grammar.v2.particle-wo-object.summary: を marks what the action directly acts on in these examples. As a particle it is written を and usually pronounced お.
grammar.v2.particle-wo-object.goal: Identify what is eaten, read or watched in an action.
grammar.v2.particle-wo-object.idea: を marks what the action directly acts on in these examples. As a particle it is written を and usually pronounced お.
grammar.v2.particle-wo-object.detail.0: Observe the relation between noun and verb: パン is what is eaten and 本 what is read. The particle follows that noun. Do not choose を just because a translation has an object: learn what relation the Japanese verb allows.
grammar.v2.particle-wo-object.detail.1: 本がある presents a book’s existence; 本を読む presents an action on that book. が and を organise different relations even with the same noun. We will develop existence later in this topic.
grammar.v2.verb-transitivity-basic.title: The door opens / someone opens the door
grammar.v2.verb-transitivity-basic.summa: In these pairs, が presents what changes and を what someone acts on: ドアが開く versus ドアを開ける.
grammar.v2.verb-transitivity-basic.goal: Distinguish a change from an action performed on something.
grammar.v2.verb-transitivity-basic.idea: In these pairs, が presents what changes and を what someone acts on: ドアが開く versus ドアを開ける.
grammar.v2.verb-transitivity-basic.detai: 開く and 開ける are not two tenses of one verb: they are a verb pair. The first sentence describes a change in the door; the second, the action of opening it. You do not need linguistic terminology to distinguish the situations.

This model is an initial tool for these pairs, not a universal rule for all transitive or intransitive sentences. Another pair is 閉まる（しまる）, close by itself, and 閉める（しめる）, close something. Learn a few pairs with their situations and patterns.
grammar.v2.location.transitivity.caption: Change and direct action
grammar.v2.particle-ni-destination.title: に — destination point
grammar.v2.particle-ni-destination.summa: In destination + に + movement verb, に marks the target point: 学校に行く.
grammar.v2.particle-ni-destination.idea: In destination + に + movement verb, に marks the target point: 学校に行く.
grammar.v2.particle-ni-destination.detai: 学校 is the target place of 行く; it is not something the verb reads or eats. The particle marks that destination role. 行く, 帰る and 来る let us practise this pattern using the plain forms from Topic 03.

に has other roles which we will study separately. Here ask “where to”. 学校へ行く can also be natural: the next lesson compares destination point with direction without treating a valid alternative as an error.
grammar.v2.particle-he-direction.title: へ — direction
grammar.v2.particle-he-direction.summary: へ marks the direction of movement and is pronounced え. 学校に行く and 学校へ行く can both be correct: destination point versus direction.
grammar.v2.particle-he-direction.goal: Express direction and read へ as a particle.
grammar.v2.particle-he-direction.idea: へ marks the direction of movement and is pronounced え. 学校に行く and 学校へ行く can both be correct: destination point versus direction.
The particle is still written へ even though it is read え. Do not change the written character when building the sentence. In this initial contrast, に highlights the destination and へ the direction towards it.

For 学校＿行く with no further restriction, we accept に and へ. If an activity specifically practises へ, the instruction will say so. Choosing に then does not make it ungrammatical: it simply does not fulfil the requested task.
grammar.v2.particle-de-action-location.s: Place + で + action marks where an activity happens. 学校に行く says where I go; 学校で勉強する says where I study.
grammar.v2.particle-de-action-location.g: Choose the location of an activity in context.
grammar.v2.particle-de-action-location.i: Place + で + action marks where an activity happens. 学校に行く says where I go; 学校で勉強する says where I study.
grammar.v2.particle-de-action-location.d: The same place can be a destination or a setting. Look at the verb and situation: going to school is movement towards it; studying there is an activity within that place.
Do not translate a preposition in your language by always choosing the same particle. Here we learn で for an action’s location; other uses of で are not this concept’s goal.
grammar.v2.particle-ni-time.title: に — marking when something happens
grammar.v2.particle-ni-time.summary: に often marks a specific time point. 今日, 明日 and 毎日 normally appear without に in basic examples.
grammar.v2.particle-ni-time.goal: Distinguish a time point from relative expressions.
grammar.v2.particle-ni-time.idea: に often marks a specific time point. 今日, 明日 and 毎日 normally appear without に in basic examples.
grammar.v2.particle-ni-time.example.3: I go today / will go tomorrow / read every day.
grammar.v2.particle-ni-time.detail.0: The hour or date before に places the action at a point. Readings are provided as support: we do not yet assess reading hours or dates. The goal is to recognise the expression’s role.
grammar.v2.particle-ni-time.detail.1: This pattern does not mean every specific time needs に. Relative expressions and some contexts work differently. At this level contrast 七時に起きる with 明日行く and avoid mechanically adding に to every time word.
grammar.v2.particle-to-companion.title: と — doing something with someone
grammar.v2.particle-to-companion.summary: Person + と + action expresses company: 友達と行く, go with a friend.
grammar.v2.particle-to-companion.goal: Identify the person accompanying an action.
grammar.v2.particle-to-companion.idea: Person + と + action expresses company: 友達と行く, go with a friend.
grammar.v2.particle-to-companion.example: I eat with my older sister.
The person before と participates with you in the situation. They are not the journey’s destination or the activity’s location. Ask “with whom” to recognise this relation.
と also joins nouns, as in パンと水, bread and water. This is another use of the same particle. This lesson assesses only company in an action.
grammar.v2.particle-kara-made.title: から・まで — from and until
grammar.v2.particle-kara-made.summary: から marks the start or origin; まで marks the limit or end. They may appear together or separately.
grammar.v2.particle-kara-made.goal: Mark origin and limit in space or time.
grammar.v2.particle-kara-made.idea: から marks the start or origin; まで marks the limit or end. They may appear together or separately.
grammar.v2.particle-kara-made.example.0: I go from home to the station.
grammar.v2.particle-kara-made.detail.0: Do not reverse the endpoints: 家から is the origin and 駅まで the limit. Time works the same way: 九時から indicates when you start and 五時まで how long the activity continues.
grammar.v2.particle-kara-made.detail.1: Either endpoint can suffice when the other is known or irrelevant. Clock readings are provided as help, not yet assessed. We focus on the relation of start and limit.
grammar.v2.existence-aru-iru.title: ある・いる — saying something exists
grammar.v2.existence-aru-iru.summary: X がある presents entities treated as non-animate; X がいる presents people or animals at this level. ある → ない is special; いる → いない.
grammar.v2.existence-aru-iru.goal: Choose ある or いる and build its plain negative.
grammar.v2.existence-aru-iru.idea: X がある presents entities treated as non-animate; X がいる presents people or animals at this level. ある → ない is special; いる → いない.
grammar.v2.existence-aru-iru.example.2: I have time, depending on context.
grammar.v2.existence-aru-iru.example.4: There is a person / Tanaka is present.
grammar.v2.existence-aru-iru.detail.0: が identifies what is presented as existing here. Choose the verb according to how the entity is treated: book or desk with ある; person or cat with いる. This が is learned within the pattern, without a separate lesson.
grammar.v2.existence-aru-iru.detail.1: Recall the note from Topic 03: the negative of ある is not formed as あらない, but ない. 時間がある naturally translates as having time, although the structure expresses existence. These are not universal literal equivalents of exist, be or have.
grammar.v2.location.existence.caption: Existence and negation
grammar.v2.location-ni-vs-de.title: に vs で — being there / doing something there
grammar.v2.location-ni-vs-de.summary: に locates existence; で places an activity. The place may be the same, but its relation to the predicate changes.
grammar.v2.location-ni-vs-de.goal: Distinguish located existence from an action in a place.
grammar.v2.location-ni-vs-de.idea: に locates existence; で places an activity. The place may be the same, but its relation to the predicate changes.
grammar.v2.location-ni-vs-de.example.0: There is a book in the library.
grammar.v2.location-ni-vs-de.example.1: I read a book in the library.
grammar.v2.location-ni-vs-de.detail.0: Seeing a place name is not enough to choose. Ask whether you present where an entity is or where it performs an activity. いる locates Tanaka; 勉強する presents what Tanaka does there.
grammar.v2.location-ni-vs-de.detail.1: The same translation with “in” may hide these two relations. In these patterns, に combines with ある or いる to locate existence and で with the action performed at the place.
grammar.v2.location.location.caption: The place’s role
grammar.v2.position-words.title: 上・下・中・前・後ろ・隣 — positions
grammar.v2.position-words.summary: Reference + の + position forms a place: 机の上. Add に and existence to locate something there.
grammar.v2.position-words.goal: Locate something relative to a reference.
grammar.v2.position-words.idea: Reference + の + position forms a place: 机の上. Add に and existence to locate something there.
grammar.v2.position-words.detail.0: の reuses the noun relation from Topic 01. 机 supplies the reference and 上 the position. The whole 机の上 phrase functions as a place before に.
grammar.v2.position-words.detail.1: 上（うえ） is above; 下（した）, below; 中（なか）, inside; 前（まえ）, in front; 後ろ（うしろ）, behind; 隣（となり）, next to. Choose the position first and then ある or いる for the entity located.
grammar.v2.question-words-basic.title: Basic question words
grammar.v2.question-words-basic.summary: 誰 asks who; 何, what; どこ, where; いつ, when; どれ, which. どの and どんな accompany a noun.
grammar.v2.question-words-basic.goal: Choose which information is missing in a question.
grammar.v2.question-words-basic.idea: 誰 asks who; 何, what; どこ, where; いつ, when; どれ, which. どの and どんな accompany a noun.
grammar.v2.question-words-basic.detail.0: The question word takes the place of the information you seek. Keep the particle for that role: 誰が identifies the person coming and 何を what is eaten. These plain questions rely on context and intonation.
grammar.v2.question-words-basic.detail.1: どれ points to an option with no following noun. どの本 asks which book; どんな本 asks what kind of book. Do not confuse selecting an option with describing its kind. We do not add a new system of question endings here.
grammar.v2.location.questions.caption: Which information you seek
grammar.v2.question-words-ka-mo.title: Something, nothing, someone and no one
grammar.v2.question-words-ka-mo.summary: 何か is something; 誰か, someone. In this pattern, 何も + negative means nothing and 誰も + negative, no one: the negation is in the predicate.
grammar.v2.question-words-ka-mo.goal: Combine question words with か or with も and negation.
grammar.v2.question-words-ka-mo.idea: 何か is something; 誰か, someone. In this pattern, 何も + negative means nothing and 誰も + negative, no one: the negation is in the predicate.
grammar.v2.question-words-ka-mo.detail.0: か joins 何 or 誰 here to form an indefinite expression. It is not a sentence-final question particle. The question in 何かある？ is understood through intonation and context, like the earlier plain questions.
grammar.v2.question-words-ka-mo.detail.1: Do not translate isolated 何も as nothing or 誰も as no one in this pattern: you need ない or いない to express negation. Learn the complete combination and distinguish things with ある from people with いる.
grammar.v2.location.indefinite.caption: A complete combination
grammar.v2.basic-counters.title: Basic counters
grammar.v2.basic-counters.summary: The number combines with a counter: つ for objects in the basic general use, 人 for people, 枚 for flat things and 本 for long objects.
grammar.v2.basic-counters.goal: Count with an appropriate unit and recognise a few special readings.
grammar.v2.basic-counters.idea: The number combines with a counter: つ for objects in the basic general use, 人 for people, 枚 for flat things and 本 for long objects.
grammar.v2.basic-counters.example.1: There are two sheets of paper.
grammar.v2.basic-counters.detail.0: The object’s shape helps choose a counter: a sheet is flat and a pencil long. In these sentences the quantity can follow が before the existence verb. We do not add requests or other new patterns.
grammar.v2.basic-counters.detail.1: Learn these complete readings: 一人 is ひとり; 二人, ふたり; 一本, いっぽん. Do not automatically combine the usual reading of each character. We work with a few common counters, without an exhaustive list of irregularities.
grammar.v2.location.counters.caption: Readings to recognise
grammar.v2.clock-time.title: Hours and minutes
grammar.v2.clock-time.summary: 時 indicates the clock hour; 分 the minutes, read ふん or ぷん depending on the number. 半 adds half an hour; 何時 asks what time.
grammar.v2.clock-time.goal: Read common clock times, half past and a question about the time.
grammar.v2.clock-time.idea: 時 indicates the clock hour; 分 the minutes, read ふん or ぷん depending on the number. 半 adds half an hour; 何時 asks what time.
grammar.v2.clock-time.example.2: I go at half past nine.
grammar.v2.clock-time.detail.0: Remember 四時 → よじ, 七時 → しちじ and 九時 → くじ. 何時 is read なんじ. For minutes, observe common examples such as 五分（ごふん） and 十分（じゅっぷん）; you need not learn every variant at once.
grammar.v2.clock-time.detail.1: 半 follows the hour: 九時半 does not mean nine hours of duration, but a clock point. To place an action, use the time pattern learned: 九時半に行く. The next part will distinguish points from amounts of time.
grammar.v2.location.clock.caption: Common clock times
grammar.v2.calendar-dates.title: Days, months and dates
grammar.v2.calendar-dates.summary: Weekdays, months and dates have their own readings. 今日, 明日 and 昨日 depend on the day you speak from; いつ asks when.
grammar.v2.calendar-dates.goal: Recognise common dates without memorising a whole calendar.
grammar.v2.calendar-dates.idea: Weekdays, months and dates have their own readings. 今日, 明日 and 昨日 depend on the day you speak from; いつ asks when.
grammar.v2.calendar-dates.detail.0: Months use number + 月: 一月（いちがつ）, January; 五月（ごがつ）, May; 四月（しがつ）, April; 七月（しちがつ）, July; 九月（くがつ）, September. For dates, learn the common readings in the table as units.
grammar.v2.calendar-dates.detail.1: Use the tables for reference and practise in stages. Memorising all 31 days at once is not required. 今日 and 明日 normally go without に; a date such as 五月三日 can mark an action’s point with に.
grammar.v2.location.dates.caption: Common dates for reference
grammar.v2.location.weekdays.caption: Days of the week
grammar.v2.duration.title: Clock time versus duration
grammar.v2.duration.summary: 二時 is two o’clock; 二時間, two hours. 二時に勉強する places the study; 二時間勉強する expresses its basic duration without に.
grammar.v2.duration.goal: Distinguish when something starts from how long it lasts.
grammar.v2.duration.idea: 二時 is two o’clock; 二時間, two hours. 二時に勉強する places the study; 二時間勉強する expresses its basic duration without に.
grammar.v2.duration.detail.0: 時 locates a clock hour; 時間 measures an amount of time. The useful question is “when” versus “for how long”. Do not translate both expressions as an hour without observing what information they supply.
grammar.v2.duration.detail.1: In the basic duration 二時間勉強する, do not add に. The quantity directly accompanies the activity. A minute expression such as 三十分 can also measure how long it lasts, depending on context.
grammar.v2.location.duration.caption: Point or amount
grammar.v2.duration-gurai.title: くらい・ぐらい — approximately
grammar.v2.duration-gurai.summary: くらい and ぐらい add approximation after a duration. They do not express duration by themselves: 二時間 supplies the time; ぐらい makes it approximate.
grammar.v2.duration-gurai.goal: Express an approximate duration with two valid variants.
grammar.v2.duration-gurai.idea: くらい and ぐらい add approximation after a duration. They do not express duration by themselves: 二時間 supplies the time; ぐらい makes it approximate.
grammar.v2.duration-gurai.example.0: I study for about two hours.
grammar.v2.duration-gurai.example.1: I read for about thirty minutes.
grammar.v2.duration-gurai.detail.0: Approximation modifies the preceding quantity. 二時間 presents two hours; 二時間くらい allows a time close to that amount. It does not turn a duration into a clock hour.
grammar.v2.duration-gurai.detail.1: In these examples くらい and ぐらい are valid alternatives. Open exercises accept both. Keep the duration pattern: 二時間ぐらい勉強する, without adding に for this basic quantity.

grammar.v2.particle-kara-made-1.prompt: Match each endpoint to its role.

grammar.v2.review05Body: Combine stem, purpose, register and context without losing the sentence’s meaning.
grammar.v2.verb-stem.title: The verb stem
grammar.v2.verb-stem.summary: First identify the family: ichidan removes る; godan changes the last kana to the い row; する → し and 来る → き.
grammar.v2.verb-stem.goal: Obtain the stem from the dictionary verb according to its family.
grammar.v2.verb-stem.idea: First identify the family: ichidan removes る; godan changes the last kana to the い row; する → し and 来る → き.
grammar.v2.verb-stem.detail.0: The stem serves ます and other constructions, such as movement purpose in the next lesson. The direction is dictionary verb → stem → construction. A stem alone is not a complete sentence here or a new conjugation to use as a predicate.
grammar.v2.verb-stem.detail.1: For ichidan keep what remains after removing る: 見る → 見 and 起きる → 起き. For godan keep the verb except the final kana, which moves to the い row. 帰る is godan: 帰り, not 帰. Learn the family with the verb rather than deciding only from a る ending.

grammar.v2.motion-purpose-ni-iku.title: Go or come to do something
grammar.v2.motion-purpose-ni-iku.summary: Form the stem first and add に + 行く / 来る: the movement’s goal is performing an action.
grammar.v2.motion-purpose-ni-iku.goal: Build the purpose of movement from the stem.
grammar.v2.motion-purpose-ni-iku.idea: Form the stem first and add に + 行く / 来る: the movement’s goal is performing an action.
grammar.v2.motion-purpose-ni-iku.example: I go to see a film.
に already marked a goal or destination. Here the goal of 行く or 来る is an action: seeing, buying or playing. Do not use the dictionary form before this purpose に: start with 見る → 見, then 見に行く.

The main verb is 行く or 来る; the preceding stem expresses why you move. After learning ます you can recognise 映画を見に行きます: 行く becomes 行きます while 見に keeps the purpose. Today’s aim is forming purpose from the dictionary verb, without removing ます from another form.
grammar.v2.polite-verb-masu-system.title: The polite ます system
grammar.v2.polite-verb-masu-system.summa: The same stem takes an ending preserving tense and polarity: these are not four new tenses, but another register.
grammar.v2.polite-verb-masu-system.goal: Combine a stem with four polite endings without losing tense or polarity.
grammar.v2.polite-verb-masu-system.idea: The same stem takes an ending preserving tense and polarity: these are not four new tenses, but another register.
grammar.v2.polite-verb-masu-system.detai: In Topic 03 you already combined affirmative/negative × non-past/past. 飲む, 飲まない, 飲んだ and 飲まなかった express those four values. Now 飲みます, 飲みません, 飲みました and 飲みませんでした preserve them and change register. They all start from 飲み.

Do not turn 飲まなかった into 飲みません when preserving past tense: you need 飲みませんでした. 飲みません is grammatical Japanese but expresses another tense. The stem of する is し; that of 来る is き. Change the ending, not the stem family.

grammar.v2.polite-desu-system.title: です with nouns and adjectives
grammar.v2.polite-desu-system.summary: Nouns and な-adjectives follow the nominal system; い-adjectives keep their conjugation and then add です.
grammar.v2.polite-desu-system.goal: Build the everyday polite system according to predicate type.
grammar.v2.polite-desu-system.idea: Nouns and な-adjectives follow the nominal system; い-adjectives keep their conjugation and then add です.
grammar.v2.polite-desu-system.detail.0: For nouns and な, connect this to 学生だ / じゃない / だった / じゃなかった. The everyday polite system uses です / じゃないです / でした / じゃなかったです. For い, conjugate the adjective first: 高かった + です, never 高いでした. Do not add だ either: 高かっただ is incorrect.
grammar.v2.polite-desu-system.detail.1: For recognition, there are more formal variants: 学生ではありません / 学生ではありませんでした; 静かではありません / 静かではありませんでした; 高くありません / 高くありませんでした. They are valid but are not the only correct forms. This lesson’s production path uses the everyday forms in the table.

grammar.v2.da-vs-desu.summary: Learn the complete form for predicate, tense, polarity and register; do not replace characters mechanically.
grammar.v2.da-vs-desu.goal: Avoid combining systems or adding だ to い-adjectives.
grammar.v2.da-vs-desu.idea: Learn the complete form for predicate, tense, polarity and register; do not replace characters mechanically.
grammar.v2.da-vs-desu.example.3: Is expensive: polite, with an い-adjective.
grammar.v2.da-vs-desu.detail.0: 学生だ and 学生です are valid forms, but 学生だです mixes both systems and is incorrect. In the past 学生だった corresponds to 学生でした: do not add another ending to produce 学生でしたった.
grammar.v2.da-vs-desu.detail.1: With い-adjectives, 高い already completes the plain predicate; 高いです adds politeness. 高いだ is not valid. This initial comparison is limited to main sentences; usage differences in more complex structures will be learned later.

grammar.v2.question-ka.title: Polite questions with か
grammar.v2.question-ka.summary: Add か to the complete polite sentence: it clearly marks the question and preserves tense and polarity.
grammar.v2.question-ka.goal: Build polite questions and reuse familiar question words.
grammar.v2.question-ka.idea: Add か to the complete polite sentence: it clearly marks the question and preserves tense and polarity.
grammar.v2.question-ka.detail.0: Start with the polite predicate, then add か. 何, どこ, いつ and 誰 select the information sought; を, に and と retain their roles. はい and いいえ are frequent responses, depending on the question.
grammar.v2.question-ka.detail.1: The mark ？ is also used in modern Japanese; it is not incorrect. Here we learn that か explicitly marks a polite question. Do not treat 行くか？ as a neutral casual version interchangeable with 行きますか: casual questions have their own nuances, to be expanded later.

grammar.v2.plain-vs-polite.summary: Change only register: preserve non-past/past, affirmative/negative and basic meaning.
grammar.v2.plain-vs-polite.goal: Compare complete systems and change only register.
grammar.v2.plain-vs-polite.idea: Change only register: preserve non-past/past, affirmative/negative and basic meaning.
grammar.v2.plain-vs-polite.example.0: I did not eat: plain, past negative.
grammar.v2.plain-vs-polite.example.1: I did not eat: polite, past negative.
grammar.v2.plain-vs-polite.example.2: This film was not interesting, politely.
grammar.v2.plain-vs-polite.detail.0: Plain forms are frequent with close people, in informal conversation and inside structures we will learn later. Polite register is often a safe choice with less familiar people, social distance and many public or professional situations. Relationship and situation matter: there is no absolute friend = plain or stranger = polite rule.

grammar.v2.sentence-ending-ne-yo.title: ね・よ・よね — sentence endings
grammar.v2.sentence-ending-ne-yo.summary: ね seeks sharing or confirmation; よ presents information or a stance with emphasis towards the listener; よね combines emphasis and seeking alignment.
grammar.v2.sentence-ending-ne-yo.goal: Choose a final communicative nuance through context.
grammar.v2.sentence-ending-ne-yo.idea: ね seeks sharing or confirmation; よ presents information or a stance with emphasis towards the listener; よね combines emphasis and seeking alignment.
grammar.v2.sentence-ending-ne-yo.example: You share an impression about the nice weather.
You share that it was interesting.
You emphasise that tomorrow is a day off.
You stress to the listener that there is no time.
You assert it is tasty and seek agreement.
ね can share an impression, seek confirmation or create agreement: it is not always literally “right?”. よ directs information or a stance towards the listener with emphasis; “new information” is only an initial approximation, not an absolute definition. Intent depends on context and tone.

ね and よ appear with plain and polite register: そうだね / そうですね. よね combines an assertion directed at the listener with seeking alignment. The usual order of the combination taught is よね, not ねよ. These initial models guide choice rather than assigning a single translation to each particle.

grammar.v2.topic06Goal: Use a sentence to describe a noun, nominalise an action, explain a situation, ask about it or quote content.
grammar.v2.review06Body: Recognise each sentence’s structure and function without changing its familiar verb forms.
grammar.v2.relative-clause-noun.title: A sentence can describe a noun
grammar.v2.relative-clause-noun.summary: The plain-form verbal clause precedes the noun and preserves tense and negation.
grammar.v2.relative-clause-noun.goal: Place a plain verbal clause before the noun it describes.
grammar.v2.relative-clause-noun.idea: The plain-form verbal clause precedes the noun and preserves tense and negation.
The book I read every day.
The book I did not buy.
grammar.v2.relative-clause-noun.detail.0: The whole description precedes 本. No mandatory word equivalent to “that” is needed. 買った keeps past, 読む non-past and 買わなかった past negative. As in Topic 05, plain form does not mean only informal conversation: it also appears inside structures. The practised pattern uses 昨日買った本, not 昨日買いました本.
grammar.v2.relative-clause-noun.detail.1: In 田中さんが買った本, Tanaka performs the action inside the description. We practise が for that internal subject without claiming は is universally impossible. Do not generalise to “any plain sentence + noun”: nouns and adjectives keep their rules, such as 日本の本 and 静かな町, not 学生だ人 or 静かだ町.
The plain-form verbal clause precedes the noun and preserves tense and negation.
A な-adjective keeps な when modifying a noun.
grammar.v2.nominalizer-no.title: Turning an action into “something”
grammar.v2.nominalizer-no.summary: の turns the action into a nominal unit that can take が or は; it does not describe a following written noun.
grammar.v2.nominalizer-no.goal: Treat an action as a nominal unit using の.
grammar.v2.nominalizer-no.idea: の turns the action into a nominal unit that can take が or は; it does not describe a following written noun.
grammar.v2.nominalizer-no.detail.0: 昨日買った本 describes a visible noun, 本. In 本を読むの, の lets us treat reading as a nominal unit. That unit can take a particle: 本を読むのが好きだ presents what is liked; 毎日勉強するのは大変だ takes the activity as topic.
grammar.v2.nominalizer-no.detail.1: Look at what precedes の: 日本語の本 links nouns, as in Topic 01; 日本語を勉強するの nominalises an action. Do not memorise an isolated translation of の. In the next lessons 本を読むんです explains a situation and 本を読むの？ asks about it: the full structure determines the function.
grammar.v2.explanatory-no-ndesu.title: のだ・んだ・のです・んです — explanation
grammar.v2.explanatory-no-ndesu.summary: んです presents explanation or context; non-past affirmative nouns and な use なんです. Other forms do not add an extra な.
grammar.v2.explanatory-no-ndesu.goal: Present information as explanation, context or background for a situation.
grammar.v2.explanatory-no-ndesu.idea: んです presents explanation or context; non-past affirmative nouns and な use なんです. Other forms do not add an extra な.
The thing is, the train was late.
The thing is, I am going tomorrow.
The thing is, it is expensive.
The thing is, I am a student.
The thing is, it is quiet.
grammar.v2.explanatory-no-ndesu.detail.0: のだ and のです present the sentence as explanation or background; んだ and んです are frequent conversational contractions. We mainly practise the latter. The difference between 電車が遅かった and 電車が遅かったんです is how information is presented in the situation, not a new tense.
grammar.v2.explanatory-no-ndesu.detail.1: Only non-past affirmative nouns and な require な here: 学生なんです and 静かなんです. Already conjugated forms add んです directly: 学生じゃないんです, 学生だったんです, 学生じゃなかったんです; likewise with 静か. 本を読むんです explains context; 本を読むのが好きだ nominalises an action. んです does not literally mean “because”: it can answer a causal question, but causal constructions will be studied later.
んです presents explanation or context; non-past affirmative nouns and な use なんです. Other forms do not add an extra な.

grammar.v2.casual-question-no.title: Contextual questions with の？
grammar.v2.casual-question-no.summary: の？ asks about a situation with contextual or confirming nuance; non-past affirmative nouns and な use なの？.
grammar.v2.casual-question-no.goal: Ask about a situation with explanatory, contextual or confirming nuance.
grammar.v2.casual-question-no.idea: の？ asks about a situation with contextual or confirming nuance; non-past affirmative nouns and な use なの？.
grammar.v2.casual-question-no.example.4: So you are not a student?
grammar.v2.casual-question-no.detail.0: You see someone preparing to leave and ask 行くの？ to confirm the situation. 行く？ also exists, but the nuance is not identical. Do not learn の？ as merely the informal version of 行きますか. Its relation to the previous explanation helps recognise its contextual function.
grammar.v2.casual-question-no.detail.1: 学生なの？ and 静かなの？ take な because they are nominal non-past affirmatives. Do not add な after other forms: 学生じゃないの？, 学生だったの？ and 行かなかったの？. Intent depends on context and intonation. This pattern need not be associated with a gender. Distinguish 本を読むのが好きだ, 本を読むんです and 本を読むの？ by their full structure, not three fixed translations of の.
grammar.v2.casual-question-no.mistake.0: の？ asks about a situation with contextual or confirming nuance; non-past affirmative nouns and な use なの？.

grammar.v2.topic07Goal: Build て from familiar families and distinguish sequence, progress, state, requests, permission and prohibition.
grammar.v2.review07Body: Choose form and function according to the verb, context and communicative intent.
grammar.v2.te-form-formation.title: How to form the て form
grammar.v2.te-form-formation.summary: The family determines the change. Use the familiar past as a shortcut: た ↔ て and だ ↔ で, without giving て past meaning.
grammar.v2.te-form-formation.goal: Form て for ichidan, godan and irregulars using the parallel with た.
grammar.v2.te-form-formation.idea: The family determines the change. Use the familiar past as a shortcut: た ↔ て and だ ↔ で, without giving て past meaning.
grammar.v2.te-form-formation.example.1: Return: godan, despite ending in る.
grammar.v2.te-form-formation.example.2: Read: the past helps form て.
grammar.v2.te-form-formation.example.3: Come: irregular form and its own reading.
grammar.v2.te-form-formation.detail.0: You already know the past た form. Change final た to て and だ to で to remember 食べた → 食べて, 買った → 買って, 読んだ → 読んで, 書いた → 書いて and 泳いだ → 泳いで. The parallel helps formation, not meaning: 食べて does not mean “I ate”. て is a connecting/base form for several structures; it is called the て form even when ending in で.
grammar.v2.te-form-formation.detail.1: From the dictionary form, ichidan removes る and adds て. For godan: う・つ・る → って; む・ぶ・ぬ → んで; く → いて; ぐ → いで; す → して. 行く is exceptional: 行って. Irregulars are する → して and 来る → 来て（きて）. Contrast 食べる → 食べて with 帰る → 帰って: family matters more than a る ending.

grammar.v2.te.formation.caption: Dictionary, familiar past and て form
grammar.v2.te-action-sequence.title: Connecting actions with て
grammar.v2.te-action-sequence.summary: In this sequence て connects actions; the final predicate determines tense and register.
grammar.v2.te-action-sequence.goal: Link actions and read tense and register in the final predicate.
grammar.v2.te-action-sequence.idea: In this sequence て connects actions; the final predicate determines tense and register.
grammar.v2.te-action-sequence.example.0: I eat breakfast and go to school.
grammar.v2.te-action-sequence.example.1: I read a book and went to bed.
grammar.v2.te-action-sequence.example.2: I drank tea and returned home, politely.
grammar.v2.te-action-sequence.detail.0: Aて、B connects actions within a sequence. 本を読んで、寝る is plain non-past; 本を読んで、寝た is plain past; 本を読んで、寝ました is polite past. 読んで stays unchanged: the last predicate locates and presents the whole sequence.
grammar.v2.te-action-sequence.detail.1: Here we practise て to connect actions. Do not turn “and then” into a universal translation: other て structures have other functions. To emphasise that one action finishes first, you will learn てから in this topic.
grammar.v2.te.sequence.caption: The final form determines tense and register
grammar.v2.te-iru-progressive.title: ている — action in progress
grammar.v2.te-iru-progressive.summary: With suitable activities, Vて + いる describes an action in progress. います changes register, not function.
grammar.v2.te-iru-progressive.goal: Describe an activity that is happening using ている.
grammar.v2.te-iru-progressive.idea: With suitable activities, Vて + いる describes an action in progress. います changes register, not function.
grammar.v2.te-iru-progressive.example.0: I am reading a book now.
grammar.v2.te-iru-progressive.example.2: I am watching a film, politely.
grammar.v2.te-iru-progressive.detail.0: First form 読んで and add いる. 読んでいる uses plain register; 読んでいます, polite. With 今 and an activity such as reading, context shows ongoing action. The activity’s time is not obtained by translating each part in isolation.
grammar.v2.te-iru-progressive.detail.1: You can recognise 読んでいない and 読んでいません as negative forms of that activity without memorising another full table now. We do not teach ている = a progressive construction as a universal equivalence. This concept practises developing activities; the next shows continuing states.
grammar.v2.te-iru-result-state.title: ている — a continuing state
grammar.v2.te-iru-result-state.summary: The verb and context can give ている the meaning of a continuing state, not an action happening now.
grammar.v2.te-iru-result-state.goal: Recognise residence, marriage and knowledge as common states.
grammar.v2.te-iru-result-state.idea: The verb and context can give ている the meaning of a continuing state, not an action happening now.
grammar.v2.te-iru-result-state.detail.0: 今、本を読んでいる shows a developing activity. 大阪に住んでいる describes residence; 結婚している, marital status; 知っている, knowledge. Do not interpret every ている as something someone is doing at this very moment.
grammar.v2.te-iru-result-state.detail.1: The initial model distinguishes developing activity and a state continuing as a result or stable situation associated with the verb. It is not an absolute rule predicting every verb. At N5, work with these common examples and their context rather than turning them into new conjugation rules.
grammar.v2.te.iruContrast.caption: Activity or state according to context
grammar.v2.te-kara.title: てから — after doing something
grammar.v2.te-kara.summary: Aてから、B emphasises A happening or finishing first and then B; main tense remains in the final predicate.
grammar.v2.te-kara.goal: Emphasise the order A first, B afterwards.
grammar.v2.te-kara.idea: Aてから、B emphasises A happening or finishing first and then B; main tense remains in the final predicate.
grammar.v2.te-kara.detail.0: ご飯を食べて、勉強する connects two actions. ご飯を食べてから、勉強する highlights finishing eating first and studying afterwards. Form て before adding から: 帰る → 帰って → 帰ってから.
grammar.v2.te-kara.detail.1: In 食べてから、勉強しました, the final form expresses polite past. てから does not require putting the first part in another past form. In this concept から belongs to the temporal てから pattern; we are not introducing a causal construction.
grammar.v2.te-kudasai.title: てください — requesting an action
grammar.v2.te-kudasai.summary: Vて + ください asks someone to perform an action: a direct polite affirmative request, dependent on context.
grammar.v2.te-kudasai.goal: Build clear affirmative requests using the て form.
grammar.v2.te-kudasai.idea: Vて + ください asks someone to perform an action: a direct polite affirmative request, dependent on context.
grammar.v2.te-kudasai.detail.0: First form the verb in て, then add ください: 見る → 見て → 見てください. Do not attach ください directly to 見る. The sentence requests an action; it does not grant permission.
grammar.v2.te-kudasai.detail.1: ください is useful for a clear polite request, but does not turn every order into an extremely delicate request. Nuance depends on relationship, situation and tone. The next lessons distinguish requesting, allowing, prohibiting and requesting that an action not be done.
grammar.v2.te-kudasai.mistake.0: Vて + ください asks someone to perform an action: a direct polite affirmative request, dependent on context.
grammar.v2.te-mo-ii.title: てもいい — permission
grammar.v2.te-mo-ii.summary: Vてもいい expresses that doing the action is allowed; add ですか to ask for that permission.
grammar.v2.te-mo-ii.goal: Give or ask permission by connecting て, いい and ですか.
grammar.v2.te-mo-ii.idea: Vてもいい expresses that doing the action is allowed; add ですか to ask for that permission.
grammar.v2.te-mo-ii.detail.0: The pattern expresses that doing A is fine or allowed. Form て and add もいい. 座ってもいい uses plain register; 座ってもいいです adds politeness; 座ってもいいですか asks permission using familiar か.
grammar.v2.te-mo-ii.detail.1: Allowing an action is not requesting it. 写真を撮ってもいいです allows photos; 写真を撮ってください requests them. Read the situation and intent before choosing, even though both are grammatical Japanese.
grammar.v2.te-mo-ii.mistake.0: Vてもいい expresses that doing the action is allowed; add ですか to ask for that permission.
grammar.v2.te-wa-ikenai.title: てはいけない — prohibition
grammar.v2.te-wa-ikenai.summary: Vて + は + いけない expresses prohibition; いけません is polite. It does not mean requesting “please do not”.
grammar.v2.te-wa-ikenai.goal: Express that an action is not allowed.
grammar.v2.te-wa-ikenai.idea: Vて + は + いけない expresses prohibition; いけません is polite. It does not mean requesting “please do not”.
grammar.v2.te-wa-ikenai.detail.0: は is a particle here and is pronounced わ. The whole pattern expresses a rule or prohibition: 食べてもいい allows eating; 食べてはいけない forbids it. The verb must be in て form before は.
grammar.v2.te-wa-ikenai.detail.1: 食べてはいけません keeps prohibition and changes to polite register. Do not confuse it with “please do not eat”: a negative request and a prohibition have different functions. The next lesson practises that contrast with the same verbs.
grammar.v2.nai-de-kudasai.title: ないでください — negative request
grammar.v2.nai-de-kudasai.summary: Start from the familiar negative ない form and add でください: a negative request, not prohibition or a “negative て” rule.
grammar.v2.nai-de-kudasai.goal: Ask someone not to do an action using the ない form.
grammar.v2.nai-de-kudasai.idea: Start from the familiar negative ない form and add でください: a negative request, not prohibition or a “negative て” rule.

grammar.v2.review08Body: Choose the construction by intent. Colloquial obligation is optional Bridge recognition.
grammar.v2.masen-ka.title: ませんか — polite invitation
grammar.v2.masen-ka.summary: Stem + ませんか invites and leaves the listener’s response open in this context.
grammar.v2.masen-ka.goal: Invite the listener to a shared action.
grammar.v2.masen-ka.idea: Stem + ませんか invites and leaves the listener’s response open in this context.
grammar.v2.masen-ka.example.1: Would you like to watch a film?
grammar.v2.masen-ka.example.2: Would you like to go tomorrow?
grammar.v2.masen-ka.detail.0: Although it contains ません, this question often works as an invitation. Start from the stem learned in Topic 05 and add ませんか. Here we do not interpret it as a simple negative.
grammar.v2.masen-ka.detail.1: 行きませんか invites with an open response; 行きましょう proposes “let’s go”. Both can be polite. Do not turn ませんか into a universal translation of “do you want...?”: context determines its use.
grammar.v2.mashou.title: ましょう — proposal
grammar.v2.mashou.summary: Stem + ましょう directly proposes a shared action. It is also polite.
grammar.v2.mashou.idea: Stem + ましょう directly proposes a shared action. It is also polite.
grammar.v2.mashou.detail.0: Add ましょう to the verb stem, not to the dictionary form or the whole ます form. The basic intent is to propose a shared action.
grammar.v2.mashou.detail.1: ませんか and ましょう do not separate polite from impolite. Here we distinguish an open invitation and a more direct proposal; there is pragmatic overlap depending on situation and intonation.
grammar.v2.mashou-ka.title: ましょうか — proposal or offer
grammar.v2.mashou-ka.summary: Stem + ましょうか asks for the listener’s reaction: shared action or offering to do it myself, depending on context.
grammar.v2.mashou-ka.goal: Consult about a shared action or offer to do something.
grammar.v2.mashou-ka.idea: Stem + ましょうか asks for the listener’s reaction: shared action or offering to do it myself, depending on context.
grammar.v2.mashou-ka.detail.0: ましょうか presents an action and seeks the listener’s reaction or decision. If both are leaving, 行きましょうか consults “shall we do it?”. If the listener carries many bags, 持ちましょうか offers “shall I do it?”.
grammar.v2.mashou-ka.detail.1: 行きませんか, 行きましょう and 行きましょうか are all valid. We practise their typical intents without absolutely rigid boundaries. Context and the relationship between speakers allow overlap.
grammar.v2.interaction.functions: Three typical intents, with contextual overlap
grammar.v2.tai.title: たい — wanting to do something
grammar.v2.tai.summary: Verb stem + たい expresses wanting to do an action; it inflects similarly to an い adjective.
grammar.v2.tai.goal: Express your own wishes and ask about the listener’s.
grammar.v2.tai.idea: Verb stem + たい expresses wanting to do an action; it inflects similarly to an い adjective.
grammar.v2.tai.example.0: I want to go to Japan.
grammar.v2.tai.example.2: What would you like to eat?
grammar.v2.tai.detail.0: Reuse the ます stem: 飲む → 飲み → 飲みたい. たい inflects similarly to an い adjective: 行きたくない, 行きたかった, 行きたくなかった. Adding です to 食べたい keeps the wish and changes register.
grammar.v2.tai.detail.1: Production focuses on your own wishes and questions to the listener. For third parties we do not assert their internal wish without context: we can rely on what they said, thought or inference. Topic 06 allows quoting: 田中さんは日本に行きたいと言った。 This is not the lesson’s central objective.
grammar.v2.hoshii.title: ほしい — wanting a thing
grammar.v2.hoshii.summary: Nがほしい expresses wanting a thing. Vたい expresses wanting to perform an action.
grammar.v2.hoshii.goal: Distinguish wanting a thing from wanting to perform an action.
grammar.v2.hoshii.idea: Nがほしい expresses wanting a thing. Vたい expresses wanting to perform an action.
grammar.v2.hoshii.detail.0: In the main pattern Nがほしい, が marks the desired thing. 水がほしい wants water; 水を飲みたい wants the action of drinking water. Also recognise ほしい in ほしくない and ほしかった without opening another exhaustive table.
grammar.v2.hoshii.detail.1: This concept is limited to wanting a thing, mainly for yourself. Do not add ほしい after a verb to express wanting to perform it: use stem + たい for that.
grammar.v2.koto-ga-dekiru.title: ことができる — being able to do something
grammar.v2.koto-ga-dekiru.summary: Dictionary verb + ことができる expresses ability or possibility. Register and negation are expressed in できる.
grammar.v2.koto-ga-dekiru.goal: Express ability with a stable construction.
grammar.v2.koto-ga-dekiru.idea: Dictionary verb + ことができる expresses ability or possibility. Register and negation are expressed in できる.
grammar.v2.koto-ga-dekiru.detail.0: The verb before こと stays in dictionary form: 話すことができる. Change the ending to できない for negation, できます for polite register and できません for polite negation. Add か to ask.
grammar.v2.koto-ga-dekiru.detail.1: You already know the idea of nominalising an action with の from Topic 06. Here we learn the stable construction with こと, without a general lesson on both nominalisers or a new potential conjugation system.
grammar.v2.obligation-standard.title: Having to do something
grammar.v2.obligation-standard.summary: From Vない, replace ない with なくて and add はいけない or はならない. Both variants express obligation.
grammar.v2.obligation-standard.goal: Express obligation with two standard variants.
grammar.v2.obligation-standard.idea: From Vない, replace ない with なくて and add はいけない or はならない. Both variants express obligation.
grammar.v2.obligation-standard.example.0: I have to take the medicine.
grammar.v2.obligation-standard.example.1: Tomorrow I have to go to school.
grammar.v2.obligation-standard.detail.0: First form the familiar negative: 勉強しない. Replace ない with なくて and add はいけない. いけません is the polite variant. 食べてはいけない forbids eating; 食べなくてはいけない requires eating: opposite functions.
grammar.v2.obligation-standard.detail.1: なくてはならない and なくてはなりません also express obligation. ならない can sound more formal or impersonal in some contexts, but we do not teach an absolute difference. Both variants belong to this single standard concept.
grammar.v2.obligation-colloquial.title: Bridge: colloquial obligation
grammar.v2.obligation-colloquial.summary: Optional Bridge: recognise ないと・なきゃ・なくちゃ as shortened obligation only in these clear contexts.
grammar.v2.obligation-colloquial.goal: Recognise shortened obligation in conversation; it is not a Core requirement.
grammar.v2.obligation-colloquial.idea: Optional Bridge: recognise ないと・なきゃ・なくちゃ as shortened obligation only in these clear contexts.
In conversation, anime and manga, parts of an obligation expression can be omitted when context recovers what is missing. If I look at the clock and need to leave, もう行かないと expresses that elliptical obligation.

Do not memorise ないと = have to as a universal equivalence: it can have other uses. Here we only recognise these shortenings in clear situations. This Bridge requires no exhaustive production and does not block Core completion; practising it keeps its own Weakness.
grammar.v2.hou-ga-ii.title: ほうがいい — advice
grammar.v2.hou-ga-ii.summary: Vた + ほうがいい advises doing; Vない + ほうがいい advises not doing. It does not impose an obligation.
grammar.v2.hou-ga-ii.goal: Advise doing or not doing an action.
grammar.v2.hou-ga-ii.idea: Vた + ほうがいい advises doing; Vない + ほうがいい advises not doing. It does not impose an obligation.
grammar.v2.hou-ga-ii.example.0: It would be better to rest.
grammar.v2.hou-ga-ii.example.1: It would be better to go to bed early.
grammar.v2.hou-ga-ii.example.2: It is better not to go.
grammar.v2.hou-ga-ii.example.3: It is better not to eat that.
grammar.v2.hou-ga-ii.detail.0: For affirmative advice use the familiar た form: 休む → 休んだ → 休んだほうがいい. た belongs to the pattern; it does not mean the advice necessarily refers to the past. For negative advice use ない: 行かないほうがいい.
grammar.v2.hou-ga-ii.detail.1: 薬を飲んだほうがいい advises taking medicine; 薬を飲まなくてはいけない expresses obligation; ここで薬を飲んではいけない forbids it here. Distinguish function and force: all are valid constructions but do not communicate the same intent.

grammar.v2.topic09: Connecting ideas and placing them in time
grammar.v2.topic09Goal: Recognise reasons, contrasts, lists and limits, and relate actions in time.
grammar.v2.review09Body: Read the whole structure and context to connect ideas and interpret temporal relations.
grammar.v2.kara-reason.title: から — giving a reason
grammar.v2.kara-reason.summary: [Reason] + から、[consequence]. In plain affirmative form, nouns and な adjectives need だ before から.
grammar.v2.kara-reason.goal: Connect a reason and consequence without confusing uses of から.
grammar.v2.kara-reason.idea: [Reason] + から、[consequence]. In plain affirmative form, nouns and な adjectives need だ before から.
grammar.v2.kara-reason.example.0: Because it is hot, I drink water.
grammar.v2.kara-reason.example.1: Because I have no time, I do not go.
grammar.v2.kara-reason.example.2: Because I am free, I read a book.
grammar.v2.kara-reason.example.3: Because it is quiet, I like this place.
grammar.v2.kara-reason.example.4: Because it is hot, I drink water: polite.
grammar.v2.kara-reason.detail.0: The reason precedes から and the consequence follows. Verbs and い adjectives connect directly; plain affirmative nouns and な adjectives keep だ: 暇だから, 静かだから. 暑いですから also shows polite connection without opening a register table.
grammar.v2.kara-reason.detail.1: Do not translate から universally as “because”. 九時から働く marks a temporal starting point; 食べてから勉強する connects a completed action with the next; 暑いから窓を開ける gives a reason. Recognise the structure before から.
grammar.v2.kara-reason.mistake.0: [Reason] + から、[consequence]. In plain affirmative form, nouns and な adjectives need だ before から.
grammar.v2.connections.kara.caption: Three structures with から
grammar.v2.node-reason.title: ので — explanatory reason
grammar.v2.node-reason.summary: ので introduces an explanatory reason. With affirmative non-past nouns and な adjectives use なので.
grammar.v2.node-reason.goal: Give a reason by presenting a circumstance.
grammar.v2.node-reason.idea: ので introduces an explanatory reason. With affirmative non-past nouns and な adjectives use なので.
grammar.v2.node-reason.example.0: Because it is raining, I stay home.
grammar.v2.node-reason.example.1: Because it is cold, I close the window.
grammar.v2.node-reason.example.2: Because it is a day off, I do not go to school.
grammar.v2.node-reason.example.3: Because it is quiet, I study here.
grammar.v2.node-reason.example.4: Because of the rain, I do not go: direct reason.
grammar.v2.node-reason.example.5: Because of the rain, I do not go: explanatory circumstance.
grammar.v2.node-reason.detail.0: Verbs and い adjectives precede ので without another copula. With an affirmative non-past noun or な adjective use な: 休みなので, 静かなので. Do not insert だ in that link.
grammar.v2.node-reason.detail.1: から often presents the reason more directly; ので often sounds more explanatory or gentle and presents a circumstance. There is much overlap: 雨だから、行かない and 雨なので、行かない can be valid depending on context. Do not reduce them to absolute subjective/objective or informal/formal oppositions.
grammar.v2.node-reason.mistake.0: ので introduces an explanatory reason. With affirmative non-past nouns and な adjectives use なので.
grammar.v2.ga-kedo-contrast.title: が・けど — connecting in contrast
grammar.v2.ga-kedo-contrast.summary: が and けど connect contrasting clauses; position distinguishes this が from the one marking an element before the predicate.
grammar.v2.ga-kedo-contrast.goal: Connect ideas with both forms and recognise the position of が.
grammar.v2.ga-kedo-contrast.idea: が and けど connect contrasting clauses; position distinguishes this が from the one marking an element before the predicate.
grammar.v2.ga-kedo-contrast.example.1: I want to go, but have no time.
grammar.v2.ga-kedo-contrast.example.2: It is quiet, but far away.
grammar.v2.ga-kedo-contrast.example.4: I want to go, but have no time: polite.
grammar.v2.ga-kedo-contrast.example.5: There is a cat: が marks the element before the predicate.
grammar.v2.ga-kedo-contrast.detail.0: In plain affirmative nouns or な adjectives keep だ before けど: 静かだけど. が often appears in polite register, and けど is very frequent in conversation with plain forms, but these are not rigid boundaries. 高いけど、おいしい and 高いですが、おいしいです are both valid.
grammar.v2.ga-kedo-contrast.detail.1: In 猫がいる, が marks the element before the predicate. In 行きたいですが、時間がありません, the first が connects clauses and the second marks 時間. The objective is A, but B; these connectors can also introduce context, soften or leave a sentence open without always literally translating as “but”.
grammar.v2.ya-open-list.title: や — open list
grammar.v2.ya-open-list.summary: AやB presents representative examples of an open list; AとB enumerates the items as a set in the basic model.
grammar.v2.ya-open-list.goal: List things as examples, not as a sequence of actions.
grammar.v2.ya-open-list.idea: AやB presents representative examples of an open list; AとB enumerates the items as a set in the basic model.
grammar.v2.ya-open-list.example.0: I buy bread, fruit and things like that.
grammar.v2.ya-open-list.detail.0: や connects nouns and presents representative items: パンや果物 leaves the list open. を after the group marks what I buy.
grammar.v2.ya-open-list.detail.1: In the basic model, と enumerates items as a set and や gives examples. We do not claim と is absolutely exhaustive in every possible context. We practise only this initial distinction.
grammar.v2.dake-only.title: だけ — only
grammar.v2.dake-only.summary: Nだけ restricts what is stated to that item: only.
grammar.v2.dake-only.goal: Understand restriction to the specified item.
grammar.v2.dake-only.idea: Nだけ restricts what is stated to that item: only.
grammar.v2.dake-only.detail.0: だけ limits the statement: 水だけ selects only water; 一人だけ restricts it to one person; 日曜日だけ limits rest days. Look at the item immediately before だけ.
grammar.v2.dake-only.detail.1: 水だけ飲む and 水だけを飲む are valid examples. We do not teach that を must always remain after だけ; the objective is to understand restriction without opening a catalogue of combinations.
grammar.v2.tari-tari.title: ～たり～たりする — representative activities
grammar.v2.tari-tari.summary: Vた + り lists representative activities; final する carries tense and register without fixing chronological order.
grammar.v2.tari-tari.goal: List activities without fixing a chronology.
grammar.v2.tari-tari.idea: Vた + り lists representative activities; final する carries tense and register without fixing chronological order.
grammar.v2.tari-tari.example.0: I read books, watch films and do things like that.
grammar.v2.tari-tari.example.1: We ate, drank and did things like that.
grammar.v2.tari-tari.example.2: I read and go to bed: sequence.
grammar.v2.tari-tari.detail.0: Add り to the familiar た form, including だ: 読んだり. Final する carries tense and register: 読んだり、見たりする; 読んだり、見たりした; 読んだり、見たりします. Do not interpret each internal た as the main tense.
grammar.v2.tari-tari.detail.1: 本を読んで、寝る connects actions in sequence; 本を読んだり、映画を見たりする gives examples of activities without fixing their chronological order. We use two たり in basic exercises to show the structure clearly, but exactly two are not always required.
grammar.v2.tari-tari.mistake.0: Vた + り lists representative activities; final する carries tense and register without fixing chronological order.
grammar.v2.mou-mada.title: もう・まだ — already / still
grammar.v2.mou-mada.summary: Here もう indicates an already completed action and まだ a continuing situation; context limits these uses.
grammar.v2.mou-mada.goal: Contrast a completed action and a continuing situation.
grammar.v2.mou-mada.idea: Here もう indicates an already completed action and まだ a continuing situation; context limits these uses.
grammar.v2.mou-mada.example.1: I have already done my homework.
grammar.v2.mou-mada.detail.0: Here もう presents a completed action and まだ a continuing situation. まだ暑い contains no ている; まだ家にいる uses existence. Recognise the whole situation, not a mandatory ending.
grammar.v2.mou-mada.detail.1: もう does not always mean “already”: it has other uses outside this topic. When asked もう食べましたか, you can answer はい、もう食べました or いいえ、まだです. The short reply is useful; the complete pending-action pattern is learned in the next concept.
grammar.v2.mada-te-inai.title: まだ～ていない — not yet
grammar.v2.mada-te-inai.summary: まだ + Vていない / Vていません expresses that an action has not yet been performed in this context.
grammar.v2.mada-te-inai.goal: Express a pending action, distinct from one still in progress.
grammar.v2.mada-te-inai.idea: まだ + Vていない / Vていません expresses that an action has not yet been performed in this context.
grammar.v2.mada-te-inai.example.1: I have not read the book yet.
grammar.v2.mada-te-inai.example.2: I have not done my homework yet.
grammar.v2.mada-te-inai.example.3: I am still reading the book.
grammar.v2.mada-te-inai.example.4: I have not read the book yet, in plain register.
grammar.v2.mada-te-inai.detail.0: Form て and add いない for plain register or いません for polite register. With まだ, in these contexts we describe the action as still pending: 食べていない, 読んでいません, していません.
grammar.v2.mada-te-inai.detail.1: まだ本を読んでいる keeps the activity ongoing; まだ本を読んでいない presents reading as not yet performed in the given context. We do not teach that まだ always requires ている: you already know まだ暑い and まだです.
grammar.v2.mae-ni.title: 前に — before
grammar.v2.mae-ni.summary: Dictionary V + 前に places B before A; with a noun use Nの前に, even when the main sentence is past.
grammar.v2.mae-ni.goal: Place an action before another using dictionary form or Nの.
grammar.v2.mae-ni.idea: Dictionary V + 前に places B before A; with a noun use Nの前に, even when the main sentence is past.
grammar.v2.mae-ni.example.1: I ate breakfast before going to school.
grammar.v2.mae-ni.example.2: I wash my hands before the meal.
grammar.v2.mae-ni.detail.0: The verb before 前に is in dictionary form even if B is past: 学校に行く前に、朝ご飯を食べた. For the pattern “before going” keep 行く前に; do not change that verb to match the main sentence’s past.
grammar.v2.mae-ni.detail.1: With a noun you need の: 食事の前に. 前 can already be a familiar physical position; here we use it for a temporal relation. The complete structure says what happens before what.
grammar.v2.ato-de.title: 後で — after
grammar.v2.ato-de.summary: Vた + 後で places B after completed A; with a noun use Nの後で. It does not imply absolute past relative to speaking time.
grammar.v2.ato-de.goal: Place B after completed A, including in future plans.
grammar.v2.ato-de.idea: Vた + 後で places B after completed A; with a noun use Nの後で. It does not imply absolute past relative to speaking time.
grammar.v2.ato-de.example.1: After returning home, I will call.
grammar.v2.ato-de.example.2: After eating, I will go out: future plan.
grammar.v2.ato-de.example.3: After class, I go to the library.
grammar.v2.ato-de.detail.0: た presents A as completed before B, not necessarily before speaking time. ご飯を食べた後で、出かけます can be a future plan. B’s ending locates the whole; with a noun use の: 授業の後で.
grammar.v2.ato-de.detail.1: 食べてから、勉強する and 食べた後で、勉強する can express A→B. てから directly connects completed A with following B; た後で places B after A. We do not claim they are always absolutely interchangeable.
grammar.v2.toki.title: とき — when
grammar.v2.toki.summary: The form before とき and context locate events: Vる normally uncompleted and Vた normally completed at the relevant point.
grammar.v2.toki.goal: Relate events according to the preceding verb, adjective or noun form.
grammar.v2.toki.idea: The form before とき and context locate events: Vる normally uncompleted and Vた normally completed at the relevant point.
grammar.v2.toki.example.0: When leaving home, I turn off the light.
grammar.v2.toki.example.1: When I got home, I called.
grammar.v2.toki.detail.0: Vる + とき normally presents the action as not yet completed at the relevant temporal point; Vた + とき normally presents it as completed there. It is not a mechanical rule of “る = before / た = after”: the verb and relationship between both events determine interpretation.
grammar.v2.toki.detail.1: 日本に行くとき、カメラを買った presents going as not yet completed at the point of buying the camera; 日本に行ったとき、カメラを買った presents it as completed at that point, during that trip. Connect an い adjective directly: 忙しいとき; use な with a な adjective: 暇なとき; use の with a noun: 学生のとき.
grammar.v2.toki.mistake.0: The form before とき and context locate events: Vる normally uncompleted and Vた normally completed at the relevant point.

grammar.v2.topic10Goal: Distinguish experience, comparison, change, choice and supposition, and follow the perspective of giving and receiving.
grammar.v2.review10Body: Relate structure and function; intention and excess are optional Bridge concepts with their own progress.
grammar.v2.experience-ta-koto-ga-aru.sum: Vた + ことがある expresses having experienced something; ことがない denies the existence of that experience.
grammar.v2.experience-ta-koto-ga-aru.goa: Express experience, lack of experience and ask about it.
grammar.v2.experience-ta-koto-ga-aru.ide: Vた + ことがある expresses having experienced something; ことがない denies the existence of that experience.
grammar.v2.experience-ta-koto-ga-aru.exa: I have been to Japan before.
Last year I went to Japan: a specific event.
I have never been to Japan.
I have never been to Japan: polite.
Have you ever been to Japan?
grammar.v2.experience-ta-koto-ga-aru.det: The familiar た form precedes ことがある. It is not simply past: 去年、日本に行った tells a specific event; 日本に行ったことがある describes life experience. あります changes register and ありますか asks about the experience.

For “I have never...” negate the existence of the experience with ことがない or ことがありません and keep the verb in た. We do not use Vなかった + ことがある as the standard “never” model: it can have other meanings and contexts, so it is not automatically declared ungrammatical.
grammar.v2.tsumori.title: Bridge: つもり — intention / plan
grammar.v2.tsumori.summary: Dictionary V / Vない + つもりだ or つもりです expresses your intention or plan without guaranteeing fulfilment.
grammar.v2.tsumori.goal: Express and recognise your own intention; optional Bridge.
grammar.v2.tsumori.idea: Dictionary V / Vない + つもりだ or つもりです expresses your intention or plan without guaranteeing fulfilment.
grammar.v2.tsumori.example.1: I intend not to go today.
grammar.v2.tsumori.example.2: I want to go to Japan: wish.
grammar.v2.tsumori.example.3: I intend to go to Japan next year.
grammar.v2.tsumori.detail.0: Use dictionary form for an affirmative intention and ない for intending not to do something. つもりだ is plain; つもりです is polite. It expresses your own plan and does not guarantee the action will happen.
grammar.v2.tsumori.detail.1: 日本に行きたい expresses a wish; 日本に行くつもりだ expresses intention. You can want something without deciding on a plan. This Bridge has basic practice and its own Weakness but is not required for Core completion.
grammar.v2.comparison-yori-hou-ga.title: より・ほうが — comparing two things
grammar.v2.comparison-yori-hou-ga.summar: Aより is the reference; Bのほうが indicates the item with more of the quality in the main pattern.
grammar.v2.comparison-yori-hou-ga.goal: Identify the reference and the item with more of a quality.
grammar.v2.comparison-yori-hou-ga.idea: Aより is the reference; Bのほうが indicates the item with more of the quality in the main pattern.
grammar.v2.comparison-yori-hou-ga.exampl: The train is faster than the bus.
I like tea more than coffee.
It would be better to rest: advice.
grammar.v2.comparison-yori-hou-ga.detail: In AよりBのほうが, A is the reference and B receives more of the quality. In バスより電車のほうが速い, the train is faster of the two; do not reverse the roles when translating.

より can appear without ほう, so we do not teach that it always needs it. The main productive pattern at this level is AよりBのほうが. 電車のほうが速い compares, while 休んだほうがいい advises: they share ほう but structure and function change.
grammar.v2.superlative-naka-de-ichiban.t: の中で・一番 — maximum within a group
grammar.v2.superlative-naka-de-ichiban.s: Define the group and use が一番 to indicate the item standing out as the maximum within it.
grammar.v2.superlative-naka-de-ichiban.g: Define a set and identify which item stands out most.
grammar.v2.superlative-naka-de-ichiban.i: Define the group and use が一番 to indicate the item standing out as the maximum within it.
grammar.v2.superlative-naka-de-ichiban.e: Among fruits, I like apples best.
Tanaka is the tallest in this class.
Which fruit do you like best?
grammar.v2.superlative-naka-de-ichiban.d: First limit the group: 果物の中で. Then highlight an item: りんごが一番好きです. The question replaces that item with 何. このクラスで also naturally defines the group’s context.
Here 一番 expresses a maximum within a set or context, not a general equivalent of “very”. Comparing two things and expressing a maximum within a group use different structures.
grammar.v2.change-naru.title: なる — reaching a state
grammar.v2.change-naru.summary: N / な adjective + になる; an い adjective replaces い with く + なる; いい → よくなる.
grammar.v2.change-naru.goal: Form changes with nouns and both adjective classes.
grammar.v2.change-naru.idea: N / な adjective + になる; an い adjective replaces い with く + なる; いい → よくなる.
grammar.v2.change-naru.detail.0: Use に with nouns and な adjectives. With い adjectives remove い and add く: 寒くなる, 高くなる. いい uses the irregular base よ: よくなる. Do not form this change with the base い.
grammar.v2.change-naru.detail.1: なる carries tense and register: 寒くなりました is polite past and 先生になった plain past. It expresses change reaching a new state without necessarily implying a conscious decision by the subject.
grammar.v2.change-naru.mistake.0: N / な adjective + になる; an い adjective replaces い with く + なる; いい → よくなる.
grammar.v2.change-naru.mistake.1: N / な adjective + になる; an い adjective replaces い with く + なる; いい → よくなる.
grammar.v2.choice-ni-suru.title: にする — choosing an option
grammar.v2.choice-ni-suru.summary: Nにする / Nにします chooses an option; Nになる describes reaching a state.
grammar.v2.choice-ni-suru.goal: Choose a thing among options, distinct from changing state.
grammar.v2.choice-ni-suru.idea: Nにする / Nにします chooses an option; Nになる describes reaching a state.
grammar.v2.choice-ni-suru.detail.0: For a choice use Nにする; にします changes to polite register. コーヒーにする chooses coffee and この本にする chooses this book. The option goes before に.
grammar.v2.choice-ni-suru.detail.1: 先生になる describes reaching a state; コーヒーにする describes choosing an option. Both structures are valid. Here we limit にする to choice without opening the general system of caused change.
grammar.v2.sugiru.title: Bridge: すぎる — too much
grammar.v2.sugiru.summary: すぎる expresses excess: verb stem, an い adjective without い or a な stem without な + すぎる; いい → よすぎる.
grammar.v2.sugiru.goal: Recognise and form basic excess; optional Bridge.
grammar.v2.sugiru.idea: すぎる expresses excess: verb stem, an い adjective without い or a な stem without な + すぎる; いい → よすぎる.
grammar.v2.sugiru.detail.0: With verbs use the ます stem: 食べすぎる, 飲みすぎる. With an い adjective remove final い: 高すぎる, 大きすぎる. With a な adjective use the stem without な: 静かすぎる. いい is irregular: よすぎる.
grammar.v2.sugiru.detail.1: とても高い means very expensive; 高すぎる means too expensive, beyond an appropriate or expected degree. すぎる is not simply “very”. This Bridge keeps basic formation and its own Weakness without blocking Core completion or opening complex negative forms.
grammar.v2.deshou-darou.title: でしょう・だろう — supposition
grammar.v2.deshou-darou.summary: でしょう is a polite supposition form; だろう is its plain/casual counterpart. Neither makes the fact certain.
grammar.v2.deshou-darou.goal: Predict with some confidence without presenting a certain fact.
grammar.v2.deshou-darou.idea: でしょう is a polite supposition form; だろう is its plain/casual counterpart. Neither makes the fact certain.
grammar.v2.deshou-darou.example.2: It will probably rain tomorrow: plain.
grammar.v2.deshou-darou.detail.0: Verbs and い adjectives connect directly to both forms. With a noun or な adjective do not insert だ before でしょう: 学生でしょう, 静かでしょう. The plain counterpart is indeed 学生だろう, 静かだろう.
grammar.v2.deshou-darou.detail.1: でしょう is often polite and だろう plain/casual, without a universal gender rule. They express supposition or probability, not certainty. Depending on context and intonation they can also seek confirmation like “right?”, but that use is not the main objective.
grammar.v2.deshou-darou.mistake.0: でしょう is a polite supposition form; だろう is its plain/casual counterpart. Neither makes the fact certain.
grammar.v2.deshou-darou.mistake.1: でしょう is a polite supposition form; だろう is its plain/casual counterpart. Neither makes the fact certain.
grammar.v2.giving-receiving.title: あげる・くれる・もらう — giving and receiving
grammar.v2.giving-receiving.summary: あげる: giving towards another person; くれる: another person gives towards my side; もらう: the subject receives from someone.
grammar.v2.giving-receiving.goal: Follow direction, subject and perspective in transfers of things.
grammar.v2.giving-receiving.idea: あげる: giving towards another person; くれる: another person gives towards my side; もらう: the subject receives from someone.
grammar.v2.giving-receiving.example.0: I gave a book to a friend.
grammar.v2.giving-receiving.example.1: My sister gave a bag to a friend.
grammar.v2.giving-receiving.example.2: A friend gave me a book.
grammar.v2.giving-receiving.example.4: I received a book from a friend, with に.
grammar.v2.giving-receiving.example.5: I received a book from a friend, with から.
grammar.v2.giving-receiving.detail.0: With あげる and くれる the subject is the giver; に marks the recipient when explicit and を the object. あげる presents giving towards another person; くれる presents a gift arriving at the speaker or someone conceptualised on their side. Translating it as “give” without perspective is insufficient.
grammar.v2.giving-receiving.detail.1: With もらう the subject is the receiver; the giver can be marked with に or から in the basic scope of people. 友達が私に本をくれた and 私は友達から本をもらった describe the same exchange, changing subject and perspective. We only transfer things: we do not teach favours with actions or requests.
